meta.title: How Jensen Huang Actually Built Nvidia
meta.working_title: He Built the Wrong Chip and Still Built the World's Most Valuable Company
meta.device: A 'DAYS OF CASH LEFT' counter in the corner that keeps nearly hitting zero (NV1 flop, Sega deal, RIVA 128), then flips into a market-value counter that climbs to $5 trillion.
meta.style: Calm serious tech-history documentary in the house 2D style. Painted plates: 1970s Kentucky boarding school, a 1990s Denny's booth under fluorescent light, a cramped early-90s office, a Tokyo boardroom, server halls glowing green. Chips as 3D props (NV1 board, RIVA 128, GeForce 256, H100). Real people as round-headed ink characters; company names as plain text, no logos.

shots.vo: A man who washed dishes at Denny's as a teenager now runs the first company in history worth five trillion dollars.
shots.visual: A teenage Jensen at a steaming dish sink; the steam clears into a $5T counter.
shots.anim: Steam rises from the sink as the boy scrubs (looping arm); the steam clears and becomes the $5T counter rolling up.

shots.vo: It started in 1993, in a booth at a Denny's in San Jose, where three engineers drank refill coffee and argued about a chip that didn't exist yet.
shots.visual: Night exterior of a roadside diner; inside, three men in a vinyl booth with coffee mugs and a notepad.
shots.anim: Night exterior of the diner, neon flicker; push through the window to three men in the booth with mugs.

shots.vo: Within a few years, their company built the wrong chip, lost almost everything, and came within about a month of running out of money.
shots.visual: Days-of-cash counter drops fast toward zero; office lights dim one by one.
shots.anim: Counter drops fast; office lights switch off one by one toward camera.

shots.vo: The chip that nearly killed it is the reason it won. And the bet that made it a giant earned almost nothing for six years.
shots.visual: Market-value counter rockets past Apple and Microsoft tiles to $5T.
shots.anim: Market value bar rockets past the Apple and Microsoft tiles; counter lands on $5T.

shots.vo: This is the story of Nvidia, and of Jensen Huang, a man who later said his will to survive exceeded almost everybody else's will to kill him.
shots.visual: Push into Jensen in his black leather jacket, backlit by a server hall.
shots.anim: Backlit by server lights; slow push in on Jensen in the leather jacket.

shots.visual: Title over a single glowing chip on a dark table.
shots.anim: A single chip glows on a dark table; title scales in; deep hit.

shots.vo: Jensen Huang was born in Taiwan in 1963. His family later moved to Thailand.
shots.visual: Parchment map: Tainan pin, then an arrow to Bangkok.
shots.anim: Pin drops on Tainan; a dotted arrow draws to Bangkok.

shots.vo: When he was nine, his parents sent him and his older brother to America, to stay with an uncle and get a good education.
shots.visual: Airport departure: two small boys with one suitcase each, parents waving.
shots.anim: Two small boys with suitcases walk to the gate; parents wave (arm loops).

shots.vo: The uncle enrolled them at a school in rural Kentucky that he thought was a prestigious boarding school.
shots.visual: Map of the USA, pin on Oneida, Kentucky; hills and a winding road.
shots.anim: US map; pin on Oneida; a winding road draws through the hills.

shots.vo: It was the Oneida Baptist Institute, a strict school that also took in troubled teenagers.
shots.visual: Painted brick dormitory in the hills, grey sky; older teenage boys in the yard.
shots.anim: Grey sky; brick dorm; older boys loiter and turn their heads toward the camera.

shots.vo: Jensen was the youngest boy in the dorm. His daily job was cleaning the bathrooms.
shots.visual: Small Jensen with a mop and bucket in a long tiled washroom.
shots.anim: Small Jensen mops a long tiled floor (mop sweep loop); echoey drips.

shots.vo: He has said he didn't complain, and that it taught him to just get on with the work in front of him.
shots.visual: Close on his determined face as he finishes the floor.
shots.anim: Push in on his determined face as he finishes; a breath.

shots.vo: His parents eventually joined them in Oregon. As a teenager he worked at Denny's, washing dishes and waiting tables.
shots.visual: Map arrow from Kentucky to Oregon; the Denny's kitchen.
shots.anim: Arrow draws from Kentucky to Oregon; dissolve into the Denny's kitchen.

shots.vo: He studied electrical engineering at Oregon State, then designed chips at AMD and LSI Logic, and took a master's degree at Stanford at night.
shots.visual: Montage: college lab, AMD and LSI office badges, a Stanford library desk at night.
shots.anim: Fast montage, 1.5 s each: college lab, badges flip in, library desk at night.

shots.vo: By the early nineties, Jensen and two engineers from Sun Microsystems, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, shared an idea.
shots.visual: The three founders in the Denny's booth; name tags pop beside each.
shots.anim: Name tags pop beside each founder as named; mugs steam.

shots.vo: Video games were moving to 3D, and ordinary computer processors couldn't keep up. Someone would build a chip just for graphics.
shots.visual: A flat 2D game sprite on an old monitor morphs into a clunky 3D shape that stutters.
shots.anim: A flat 2D sprite morphs into a clunky 3D shape that stutters (frame skips).

shots.vo: They founded Nvidia in April 1993, with about forty thousand dollars between them.
shots.visual: Incorporation papers on the diner table next to the coffee.
shots.anim: Papers slide onto the table next to the coffee; a pen signs.

shots.vo: Their first chip, the NV1, came out in 1995. It tried to do everything at once: graphics, sound and game controller support on one card.
shots.visual: 3D NV1 card rotates on a workbench, components labeled.
shots.anim: The NV1 card rotates on the bench; part labels draw on with leader lines.

shots.vo: It also drew 3D shapes in an unusual way, using curved surfaces called quadratic patches.
shots.visual: On a monitor, a 3D model built from smooth curved patches.
shots.anim: A model builds from smooth curved patches on the monitor.

shots.vo: Then Microsoft released DirectX, the standard most PC games would be built on. And DirectX was built around triangles.
shots.visual: A wall of game boxes all showing triangle meshes; the curved model looks out of place.
shots.anim: A wall of triangle-mesh game boxes; the curved model slides in and looks out of place.

shots.vo: Nvidia had bet the company on the opposite approach. Jensen later said they built the wrong thing with great confidence.
shots.visual: The NV1 card on a shelf gathering dust; returns piled in boxes.
shots.anim: Dust settles on the shelved card; return boxes stack up with thuds.

shots.vo: The NV1 sold badly. Money was running out.
shots.visual: Days-of-cash counter tumbles.
shots.anim: Counter tumbles; low drone.

shots.vo: Nvidia had one lifeline: a contract with Sega to build the graphics chip for its next game console.
shots.visual: A signed contract on a desk with SEGA in plain letters.
shots.anim: Signed contract slides onto the desk; light warms.

shots.vo: But that chip was based on the same curved-surface design, the one the rest of the industry was abandoning.
shots.visual: Engineers stare at a whiteboard with a curved model crossed out.
shots.anim: Engineers stare at the whiteboard; the curved model gets crossed out with a marker squeak.

shots.vo: If they finished it, they'd spend a year building something dead. If they quit, they'd lose their only paying customer.
shots.visual: Jensen alone in a dark office, the counter glowing near zero.
shots.anim: Dark office; only the counter glows near zero; slow push in.

shots.vo: So Jensen flew to Japan and did something unusual. He told Sega's chief executive, Shoichiro Irimajiri, that Nvidia's approach was wrong, and that Sega should find another partner.
shots.visual: Tokyo boardroom, rain on tall windows; Jensen bows before Irimajiri.
shots.anim: Rain on tall windows; Jensen bows slowly; Irimajiri watches.

shots.vo: Then he asked for the rest of the money anyway. As an investment, not a payment, because without it Nvidia would go under.
shots.visual: A cheque-shaped card reading $5,000,000 floats between them.
shots.anim: The cheque card floats up between them and turns.

shots.vo: Irimajiri agreed. Jensen has said the only reason was that Irimajiri liked him.
shots.visual: Irimajiri nods slowly; a faint smile.
shots.anim: Irimajiri nods slowly; a faint smile.

shots.vo: That five million dollars bought Nvidia about six months.
shots.visual: Days-of-cash counter jumps up to ~180, then begins ticking down again.
shots.anim: Counter jumps up to about 180 with a lift, then starts ticking down again.

shots.vo: Nvidia laid off much of its staff and threw everything at one new chip, built around triangles and DirectX.
shots.visual: Half-empty office; remaining engineers hunched over boards late at night.
shots.anim: Half-empty office at night; heads bent over boards; a clock ticks.

shots.vo: To save time they bought an emulator, a machine that let them test the design in software before any real chip existed.
shots.visual: A big 3D emulator box hums in the corner, cables everywhere.
shots.anim: Big emulator hums in the corner; cables sway; LEDs blink.

shots.vo: They had roughly a month of payroll left when the chip went to the factory.
shots.visual: Days-of-cash counter at 30.
shots.anim: Counter sits at 30 in red; heartbeat SFX.

shots.vo: It was called the RIVA 128, released in 1997. And this time it worked.
shots.visual: 3D RIVA 128 chip lifts off its board, light sweeping across it.
shots.anim: The chip lifts off its board in 3D; a light sweep crosses it.

shots.vo: It sold about a million units in its first four months.
shots.visual: A stack of chip boxes grows to 1,000,000.
shots.anim: Boxes stack up fast; counter to 1,000,000.

shots.vo: For years afterwards, Jensen opened staff meetings with the same line: our company is thirty days from going out of business.
shots.visual: Jensen at a whiteboard; behind him the words 'THIRTY DAYS'.
shots.onscreen: '30 DAYS FROM GOING OUT OF BUSINESS'
shots.anim: Jensen taps the whiteboard; the words write themselves behind him.

shots.vo: In 1999, Nvidia went public, and launched the GeForce 256.
shots.visual: Stock exchange ticker with NVDA; a gaming PC opens to reveal the card.
shots.anim: Ticker scrolls NVDA; the PC side panel swings open to reveal the card.

shots.vo: It marketed the chip with a new name: the GPU, the graphics processing unit.
shots.visual: Callout card with the three letters.
shots.anim: Callout card; the three letters stamp in one at a time.

shots.vo: The GeForce took over 3D calculations that used to fall on the computer's main processor. Games got smoother, lighting got better, worlds got bigger.
shots.visual: Side by side game frame: blocky 1998 scene vs richer 1999 scene.
shots.anim: Split wipe: blocky scene vs richer scene.

shots.vo: By the early 2000s, Nvidia was the leading name in PC graphics. Gamers, game studios and film effects houses all ran on it.
shots.visual: Montage: LAN party, game studio desks, a VFX artist's screen.
shots.anim: Fast montage: LAN party, studio desks, VFX screen; each 1 s.

shots.vo: Nvidia also won the deal to supply the graphics chip for Microsoft's first Xbox in 2001.
shots.visual: Painted living room with a big black console under a TV.
shots.anim: Living room; the console sits under the TV; game light flickers on the walls.

shots.vo: Nvidia won partly through speed. Jensen pushed the team to ship a new generation of chips roughly every six months, while rivals took a year or more.
shots.visual: A calendar flips; new chip boxes pop out every six months on Nvidia's side, slower on the rival's side.
shots.anim: Calendar flips; new chip boxes pop out on Nvidia's side twice as often as the rival's.

shots.vo: Its biggest rival, 3dfx, the maker of the Voodoo cards that gamers had loved, couldn't keep up.
shots.visual: A rival office with VOODOO posters goes dark, one light at a time.
shots.anim: Rival office lights go dark one at a time.

shots.vo: At the end of 2000, Nvidia bought what was left of 3dfx. Five years after the NV1 flop, Nvidia was the company others were trying to catch.
shots.visual: Nvidia staff carry boxes labeled 3DFX PATENTS into their office.
shots.anim: Staff carry 3DFX PATENTS boxes in (carry walk cycles).

shots.vo: Here's the difference that changed everything. A normal processor is like one very smart worker doing tasks one after another, very fast.
shots.visual: One ink figure works through a stack of papers at speed.
shots.anim: One figure stamps through a paper stack at speed.

shots.vo: A GPU is like thousands of simple workers, each doing one small calculation at the same time.
shots.visual: Pull back: a vast hall of tiny figures each stamping one sheet at once.
shots.anim: Pull back to reveal a vast hall of tiny figures stamping at once.

shots.vo: For graphics, that's perfect: every pixel can be worked on at once. But lots of other problems look the same. Weather. Chemistry. Physics.
shots.visual: The hall's papers turn into weather maps, molecules, fluid swirls.
shots.anim: The papers turn into weather maps, molecules and fluid swirls.

shots.vo: In 2006 Nvidia announced CUDA, software that let scientists program its graphics chips for any kind of calculation.
shots.visual: Code on a dark screen with the word CUDA.
shots.anim: Code types onto a dark screen; CUDA glows.

shots.vo: It was expensive. Every chip had to carry extra hardware for it, and for years, hardly anyone paid for it.
shots.visual: A finance chart with costs climbing and a flat CUDA revenue line; worried executives.
shots.anim: Costs climb, revenue line flat; executives glance at each other.

shots.vo: Wall Street didn't like it. Nvidia's share price fell hard after 2008. Jensen kept funding CUDA anyway, and gave it to universities.
shots.visual: Stock line falls; Jensen hands a box of GPUs to a professor.
shots.anim: Stock line falls behind him; Jensen hands a box of GPUs to a professor.

shots.vo: In 2008 things got worse. A manufacturing defect in some laptop chips forced Nvidia to set aside about two hundred million dollars, and the financial crisis hit at the same time.
shots.visual: A pile of returned laptops; a ledger with a red -$196M entry.
shots.anim: Returned laptops pile up; red ledger entry writes in.

shots.vo: From its 2007 peak, the stock lost more than three quarters of its value. Investors asked why Nvidia was spending so much on a product almost nobody used.
shots.visual: Share price line drops from a peak to a deep valley.
shots.anim: Price line drops from the peak into a deep valley.

shots.vo: He was betting that somewhere, some researcher would find a job only this kind of chip could do.
shots.visual: A university lab at night, one student working under a desk lamp.
shots.anim: University lab at night; one student under a lamp; quiet.

shots.vo: In 2012, that job arrived. It came from the University of Toronto.
shots.visual: Snowy Toronto campus at night; a lit window.
shots.anim: Snow falls; one lit window; slow push.

shots.vo: A contest called ImageNet asked computer programs to recognise objects in more than a million photos.
shots.visual: A grid of photos: cats, cars, mushrooms, boats, each with a guessing label.
shots.anim: Photo grid pops in; guessing labels flicker between options.

shots.vo: Most teams hand-designed the features the computer should look for. Edges, textures, shapes.
shots.visual: Researchers drawing edge and texture filters on a chalkboard.
shots.anim: Filters draw on the chalkboard as she points.

shots.vo: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton did something different. They built a deep neural network and let it learn from the data itself.
shots.visual: Three ink figures at a desk; a layered network diagram grows behind them.
shots.anim: A layered network diagram grows layer by layer behind them.

shots.vo: Training it took an enormous number of small calculations at once. They ran it on two Nvidia gaming cards, in a bedroom.
shots.visual: Two 3D GeForce GTX 580 cards side by side in a PC, fans spinning.
shots.anim: Two cards in a PC, fans spinning, slight rotation.

shots.vo: The best rival entry got about twenty-six percent of its top answers wrong. Their network, AlexNet, got about fifteen percent wrong.
shots.visual: Bar chart: 26.2% vs 15.3% error.
shots.anim: Two error bars grow; the AlexNet bar stops much lower; hit.

shots.vo: In a field where progress came in tiny steps, it was a leap. And it ran on Nvidia.
shots.visual: The two cards glow; the counter changes from DAYS OF CASH to MARKET VALUE.
shots.anim: Cards glow; the counter label flips and starts climbing.

shots.vo: Within a few years, almost every serious AI lab was buying Nvidia chips. The hobby nobody wanted had found its customer.
shots.visual: Labeled buildings light up one by one: GOOGLE, MICROSOFT, META, STANFORD, MIT.
shots.anim: Buildings light up one by one as named.

shots.vo: Jensen moved fast. Nvidia began building whole AI computers, not just cards.
shots.visual: 3D DGX-1 box, gold front panel, on a pedestal.
shots.anim: The DGX-1 rises on a pedestal; gold panel shines.

shots.vo: In 2016 he personally delivered the first one to a small non-profit lab in San Francisco called OpenAI. He signed it: to the future of computing and humanity.
shots.visual: Jensen carries the box through an office door; staff gather; a marker signature on the lid.
shots.anim: Jensen carries the box in; staff gather; a marker signature draws on the lid.

shots.vo: Nvidia designs its chips, but doesn't make them. Most are manufactured by TSMC in Taiwan.
shots.visual: Painted TSMC fab in Hsinchu, clean-room workers in white suits.
shots.anim: Clean-room workers in white suits move slowly; yellow light.

shots.vo: In 2020, Jensen tried to buy Arm, the British company whose chip designs sit inside almost every smartphone, for forty billion dollars.
shots.visual: A deal card '$40B' between NVIDIA and ARM text tiles; a phone opens to show an Arm core.
shots.anim: Deal card slides between the tiles; the phone opens to show an Arm core.

shots.vo: The rest of the industry objected. Regulators in America, Britain and Europe opened investigations, and the US Federal Trade Commission sued to block it.
shots.visual: Three government buildings, each stamping a document.
shots.anim: Three buildings each stamp a document (three stamp hits).

shots.vo: In 2022, Nvidia gave up on the deal.
shots.visual: The deal card tears in half.
shots.anim: The deal card tears in half; paper rip SFX.

shots.vo: That same year, the US government banned Nvidia from selling its top AI chips, the A100 and H100, to China.
shots.visual: A Washington memo stamped 'EXPORT CONTROL'; crates of chips stopped at a port.
shots.anim: Memo stamped; crates stop at the port; a barrier drops.

shots.vo: Nvidia designed slower versions to fit inside the rules, like the H800. In 2023, Washington tightened the rules and those were blocked too.
shots.visual: A modified chip slides through a gate, then a second gate slams shut.
shots.anim: A modified chip slides through the first gate; the second gate slams shut.

shots.vo: Nvidia was no longer just a chip company. It had become part of a technology contest between the world's two biggest powers.
shots.visual: A chessboard with US and China pieces; the GPU sits in the middle as a piece.
shots.anim: Chessboard; pieces slide; the GPU sits in the middle as a piece.

shots.vo: Then, in late 2022, ChatGPT launched, and every tech company on Earth wanted to build its own AI.
shots.visual: A chat window glows on a laptop; crowds of companies rush toward a server hall.
shots.anim: A chat window glows; crowds of company tiles rush toward the server hall.

shots.vo: Training those models takes vast data centres full of GPUs. Nvidia's chips, and its CUDA software, were the standard.
shots.visual: Endless rows of server racks with green lights.
shots.anim: Endless racks with green lights; slow push down the aisle.

shots.vo: Seventeen years of CUDA meant that most AI code was already written for Nvidia. Switching to a rival chip wasn't just buying new hardware; it meant rewriting software.
shots.visual: A huge library of code books all stamped CUDA; a rival chip sits alone with an empty shelf.
shots.anim: Library of code books stamped CUDA; the rival chip sits by an empty shelf.

shots.vo: Nvidia's value climbed in leaps. One trillion dollars in 2023. Three trillion in 2024. Four trillion in July 2025.
shots.visual: Staircase chart with labeled steps $1T, $3T, $4T.
shots.anim: A staircase draws step by step with labels.

shots.vo: Its newer Blackwell chips were sold out long before the factories could make enough of them.
shots.visual: 3D Blackwell board on a pedestal; an order queue scrolls beside it.
shots.anim: Board rotates on a pedestal; the order queue scrolls.

shots.vo: On the twenty-ninth of October 2025, Nvidia became the first company ever worth five trillion dollars.
shots.visual: Market-value counter lands on $5T; confetti of tiny chips.
shots.anim: Counter lands on $5T; tiny chip confetti falls.

shots.vo: From a diner booth, a dead-end chip, a favour from Sega, a chip finished with thirty days of cash, and a science project nobody paid for.
shots.visual: Recap strip: Denny's booth, NV1, Tokyo bow, RIVA 128, Toronto lab.
shots.anim: Recap strip slides past: booth, NV1, Tokyo bow, RIVA 128, Toronto lab.

shots.vo: Every one of those bets looked mad at the time. Jensen kept making them.
shots.visual: Jensen walks into a vast server hall, leather jacket, alone.
shots.anim: Jensen walks alone into the hall (walk cycle); camera follows.

shots.vo: He still runs the company his own way. He has around sixty people reporting directly to him, few one-on-one meetings, and he still talks about the company as if it could die tomorrow.
shots.visual: Jensen in a large open meeting with dozens of staff around a long table.
shots.anim: Open meeting; staff around a long table; he gestures; heads turn.

shots.vo: If you want to see who ends up owning a slice of a company like this, watch our story on BlackRock next.
shots.visual: End card with the channel name.
shots.anim: End card; music resolves.

hooks: A dishwasher from Denny's runs the first $5 trillion company in history. The chip that almost killed it is the reason you should never trust a sure thing.
Nvidia built the wrong chip, lost its only customer, and was 30 days from going out of business. Then Jensen Huang flew to Tokyo and asked the client he was quitting for $5 million.

fixes: Added (not in transcript): six-month product cycle, 3dfx asset purchase (Dec 2000), 2008 laptop-chip defect charge (~$196M) and share-price fall, DGX-1 hand-delivered to OpenAI (2016), CUDA software lock-in, $1T (2023), $3T (2024), $4T (July 2025) milestones, ~60 direct reports.
'$5 empire' fixed to $5 trillion; Nvidia passed $5T market value on 29 Oct 2025.
'$20 every single hour' is garbled; dropped.
Founding: April 1993 (transcript said the pitch was in 1992; the idea was discussed in late 1992). Co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem named; transcript left them out.
Oneida: Jensen's uncle thought it was a prestigious school; it was a strict Baptist boarding school that took troubled kids. He cleaned bathrooms. Kept factual, no 'reform school' label.

Sega: the contract was for Sega's next console chip (NV2). Sega's Dreamcast ended up using another company's graphics chip, so 'the Dreamcast' is dropped. CEO Shoichiro Irimajiri agreed to pay the remaining $5M as an investment; Jensen says it kept Nvidia alive about six months.
RIVA 128: 1997, about 1 million units in four months. Nvidia used an emulator to save time. 'About a month of payroll' matches Jensen's own accounts.
'Wrote one word on the whiteboard: More' dropped: not sourced. Replaced with his real catchphrase, 'Our company is thirty days from going out of business'.
GeForce 256 (1999) was marketed as the world's first GPU. Nvidia IPO January 1999.
CUDA: announced 2006. The '$500 million' figure isn't solidly sourced; script says it was expensive and barely earned money for years.
AlexNet 2012: 15.3% top-5 error vs 26.2% for the runner-up; trained on two GTX 580 cards. Team named (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton).
Arm: announced September 2020, $40B; FTC sued December 2021; UK and EU investigated; deal abandoned February 2022. The UK did not formally block it, so 'the UK blocked it' is changed.
China: A100/H100 export ban in 2022; H800 made to fit the rules; blocked again in October 2023.
Closing quote is 'my will to survive exceeds almost everybody else's will to kill me' (transcript dropped 'almost').
All comic dialogue in the transcript replaced with narration, to keep the calm documentary tone.
cuts: BetterHelp sponsor read removed in full.
Joke dialogue scenes (fictional quotes from staff, ImageNet announcer, regulators) removed.
